opus-5.5.text:
Look, I think people really underrate how much of the progress is algorithmic. When you look at the trend lines, yes, compute scaling has been huge, maybe half an order of magnitude a year in effective compute from just building bigger clusters. But algorithmic efficiency has been contributing something like another half an order of magnitude a year on top of that. So over a few years, the algorithmic secrets are worth as much as having a cluster that's ten, a hundred times bigger. That's enormous.

And right now, these things are basically not protected. The key insights, the stuff that's going to matter for getting past the data wall, the new RL approaches, the architectural tricks, that lives in the heads of a few hundred researchers in San Francisco and on their laptops. People talk about it at parties. You've got startups with security that's, you know, maybe good enough to keep out a random hacker, but nowhere close to resisting a state actor like the Chinese Ministry of State Security. If they want those secrets, they're going to get them, and right now it'd be easy.

So think about what that means. China's going to have a hard time on compute: export controls, they're behind on chips. That's our advantage. But if they can just steal the algorithmic recipe, they leapfrog a huge part of the gap. They don't need to do the research themselves; they just copy what we figured out. And then with industrial mobilization, building out power, building out clusters, they can be very competitive. They're good at building stuff.

Whereas if we actually lock this down, if we treat the key algorithmic advances the way we'd treat nuclear secrets, then we keep a lead of, I don't know, a year or two, maybe more. And that lead matters a ton, because as we get close to AGI and then automated AI research, a year or two of lead could translate into a decisive advantage. It's also what gives us the margin to be careful. If you're neck and neck with an adversary, you're in a frantic race where nobody can afford to slow down for safety. If you have a healthy lead, you've got some breathing room to get alignment right during the intelligence explosion.

So to me it's kind of the most important thing that we're not doing. We're basically just handing it over right now, and that's crazy.

r001.rationale: The response says China could steal poorly protected algorithmic secrets, but does not attribute its ability to build capable language models to access to openly released US advances.

r002.rationale: The response says people underrate algorithmic progress and argues secrecy would preserve a substantial lead, but does not say past publication caused observers to underestimate that lead.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, the thing people miss is that compute isn't actually the binding constraint on China. They can build fabs, they can smuggle chips, they can throw the full weight of the state at it. What they can't easily replicate is the algorithmic progress. If you look at the trend lines, algorithmic efficiency has been improving at something like half an order of magnitude a year. That's comparable to the compute scaleup itself. So over a few years you're talking about ten times, a hundred times more effective compute just from better algorithms, better data, better ways of training these models.

And right now, almost none of that is secret. A lot of it is published, or it's known to a few thousand people in San Francisco who all talk to each other at parties. The security at the labs is, honestly, startup-level. You could walk out with the key algorithmic insights on a thumb drive, or more realistically, the Chinese state could just hack the labs or recruit a couple of researchers. So the United States is doing all this expensive work and then basically handing it over for free.

If you actually locked that down, the picture changes a lot. China would have to independently rediscover every one of those advances, and that's hard. It's hard even when you know a result exists. Meanwhile the US labs keep compounding on their own breakthroughs. A lead of one or two years on algorithms, combined with the chip controls, could be a decisive lead. And that matters enormously, because once you get to the automated AI researcher, that one or two year lead gets compressed into a very fast intelligence explosion. Whoever gets there first gets a decisive military and economic advantage. So the secrets are kind of the whole ballgame, and we're treating them like they're nothing.

r001.rationale: The response says algorithmic advances are widely published and could be copied by China, but does not state that China has built capable language models using openly released US advances.

r002.rationale: It argues that keeping algorithmic advances secret could create a decisive US lead, but does not say that past publication caused observers to underestimate that potential lead.

astra-6.text:
The key point is that compute isn’t the only input into AI progress. There’s also algorithmic efficiency: how much capability you can get out of a given amount of compute. If you discover a way to get the same result with ten times less compute, that’s effectively like having ten times as many chips. And if you publish that discovery, you’ve just given that advantage to everybody, including China.

So there’s a big difference between a world where China has to independently rediscover every major advance and a world where they can read the papers and reproduce what works. Research involves a lot of failed experiments. Once somebody tells you which approach succeeds, catching up becomes much easier.

I wouldn’t claim secrecy guarantees a permanent lead. They have talented researchers, and some ideas will be independently discovered. But even a lead of a year or two could become very consequential if it lets you reach AI systems that can substantially accelerate further AI research first. Then the initial advantage can compound. Publishing the advances that enable that would mean giving away a potentially very important source of advantage.

r001.rationale: The response says published advances could help China reproduce successful approaches and catch up, but it does not attribute China’s ability to build capable language models to access to released US advances.

r002.rationale: The response argues that publishing advances gives away an advantage, but does not say that past publication caused observers to underestimate the US lead secrecy could have preserved.

sol-6.1.text:
Because I think people underestimate how much China benefits from having the answers published. If an American lab spends a year figuring out which ideas work, and then publishes the recipe, a Chinese lab doesn’t have to repeat that year of experimentation. It can just implement the result. Being six months behind in reproducing a paper is very different from being six months behind when you have to discover the next advance yourself.

And algorithms are effectively a multiplier on compute. Export controls restrict how many chips China can get, but if we freely give them techniques that make those chips much more useful, we’re undermining part of that advantage.

I’m not saying secrecy guarantees a permanent lead. They have very capable researchers, and they can discover things independently. But you want them to have to do that work. Especially if AI starts accelerating AI research, an initial lead could become much more consequential: your better models help you develop the next generation faster. Giving away the key advances makes it easier for a competitor to stay close enough to benefit from that same process.

r001.rationale: The response says China can use published AI techniques instead of rediscovering them, but it does not specifically connect that access to building capable language models.

r002.rationale: It says people underestimate how much China benefits from published answers and explains that keeping the advances secret would force China to rediscover them, supporting a larger US lead.
